Sorting numbers changes their average.

questions.stem: The class counts 8 seeds in a red cup and 5 in a blue cup. How many seeds are there altogether?
hints: Combine both cup counts.
questions.explanation: Eight from the first cup plus five from the second gives 13.
questions.misconception: The same objects may be counted twice in a total.

questions.stem: A pupil records 4, 0 and 6 visitors over three mornings. How many mornings are represented in the data?
hints: A day with no visitors is still a recorded day.
questions.explanation: There is one value for each morning, including the zero, giving three observations.
questions.misconception: The number of written entries always equals the number of valid observations.

questions.stem: A total of 12 exercise books is shared equally between two groups. What is the average number of books per group?
hints: Picture two equal piles.
questions.explanation: Split the total of 12 into two equal groups. Each share is 6.
questions.misconception: The largest value gives the mean.

questions.stem: The three height readings are 10, 6 and 8 cm. When arranged from smallest to largest, which number comes first?
hints: Compare all three readings before putting one first.
questions.explanation: The order is 6, 8, 10. The first reading in that order is 6 cm.
questions.misconception: Sorting changes the measured values.

hints: Both baskets contribute to the result.
questions.explanation: Count the contents of each basket once. Seven plus nine is 16.
questions.misconception: The same objects may be counted twice in a total.

questions.stem: Three pupils count 4, 5 and 9 bottle tops. What is the average count per pupil?
hints: Find the combined count before sharing it equally.
questions.explanation: The total is 18. Dividing it among three pupils gives an average of 6.
questions.misconception: The largest value gives the mean.

questions.stem: A class records 12, 0, 8 and 4 trees on four plots. What is the total number recorded?
hints: Include every plot, even the empty one.
questions.explanation: Twelve plus zero plus eight plus four gives 24 trees.
questions.misconception: The same objects may be counted twice in a total.

hints: Separate a missing measurement from a measured zero.
questions.explanation: Three days have recorded values. Wednesday contributes no measured value.
questions.misconception: The number of written entries always equals the number of valid observations.

hints: Check whether the values changed or only their positions.
questions.explanation: Both rows contain the same four counts. Their sum is 26 in either order.
questions.misconception: Sorting changes the measured values.

questions.stem: The class counted 10, 14 and 12 visitors at three stalls. What is the mean number for a stall?
hints: Share the total across the stalls observed.
questions.explanation: The total is 36. There are three stalls, so the mean is 12 visitors.
questions.misconception: The largest value gives the mean.

hints: Count the day on which no pages were read.
questions.explanation: The pupil read nine pages over three recorded days. Nine divided by three is three.
questions.misconception: The largest value gives the mean.

questions.stem: Arrange the counts 8, 2 and 5 on paper. What is the sum of the two smallest counts?
hints: Sort before selecting the two requested values.
questions.explanation: The sorted list is 2, 5, 8. The two smallest values add to 7.
questions.misconception: Sorting changes the measured values.

hints: Remove only the extra counts.
questions.explanation: The recorded total is 35. Removing two duplicate counts leaves 33.
questions.misconception: The same objects may be counted twice in a total.

hints: Update all three trays before calculating.
questions.explanation: There were 24 seeds. Six more make 30, and 30 divided by three is 10.
questions.misconception: The largest value gives the mean.

questions.explanation: One entry is a duplicate. Six entries minus one extra copy leaves five observations.
questions.misconception: The number of written entries always equals the number of valid observations.

hints: Keep both valid fives when sorting the corrected readings.
questions.explanation: After correction, the four readings total 20. Dividing by four gives a mean of 5.
questions.misconception: Sorting changes the measured values.

questions.explanation: Twenty-seven cards came from three classes. Each class contributed nine on average.
questions.misconception: The largest value gives the mean.

questions.explanation: Four times six gives 24 seeds. The known pots contain 15, leaving 9 for the fourth.
questions.misconception: The largest value gives the mean.

questions.explanation: The three counts sum to 40. Subtract four books included twice to obtain 36.
questions.misconception: The same objects may be counted twice in a total.

questions.explanation: Both orders have total 18 and three entries. Each gives a mean of 6 because reordering does not change either part of the calculation.
questions.misconception: Sorting changes the average.

criteria.description: Shows the original and a correctly sorted version of the same three counts.
Calculates the total of 18 and the mean of 6 for both orders.
Explains why reordering leaves the mean unchanged.
